chunks: How BLDC motors work. The question: How do BLDC motors work?
A brushless DC motor puts the magnets on the spinning part and the coils on the fixed part. Because the coils never move, no brushes are needed to feed them.
Instead, electronics switch the current through the coils in a repeating order, and the magnet on the rotor keeps chasing the moving magnetic field.
Picture a carrot on a stick held in front of a donkey. The donkey keeps walking toward the carrot, and you keep moving the stick a little ahead.
The rotor magnet is the donkey, and the changing field from the coils is the carrot.
The analogy has a gap: the controller must know where the rotor is, so it knows when to move the carrot.
The BLDC control loop in one picture. The rotor moves, the position code changes, and the controller steps the stator field forward again.
Nothing mechanical decides when to switch.
Stator: the fixed part holding the coils. Rotor: the spinning part holding the permanent magnets. Phase: one of the three groups of coils, usually named A, B and C.
Hall sensor: a sensor that detects the rotor magnet's position. Commutation: switching which coils are powered, here done by electronics. Compare "What are brushes?"
Power two of the three phases. This makes a magnetic field pointing in one direction, and the rotor magnet swings to line up with it.
Just before it arrives, the controller powers a different pair of phases. The field jumps ahead by 60 electrical degrees, and the rotor follows.
(On the simplest motor, with one pair of magnet poles, electrical degrees equal real degrees of turn.)
There are six such steps, and 6 times 60° = 360° makes one electrical revolution. That is the whole idea: switch the field ahead of the rotor, again and again.
"A BLDC motor has permanent magnets on the rotor and three coils on the stator, so there's no brush or commutator.
An electronic inverter energises two of the three phases at a time to create a stator field, and steps to the next pair every 60 electrical degrees so the rotor keeps chasing the field.
It knows the rotor position from Hall sensors or from back-EMF.
So it's really a three-phase synchronous motor, but because the torque goes with current and speed goes with voltage, it behaves like a DC motor."
